source_text: Πρόκειται οὖν νῦν τὴν οὕτως ἔχουσαν αὐτοῦ ἀνατρέψαι λέξιν· θεὸς μὲν. ὦ Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Χριστιανοὶ, καὶ θεοῦ παῖς οὐδεὶς οὔτε κατῆλθεν οὔτε κατέλθοι. εἰ δέ τινας ἀγγέλους φατὲ, τίνας τούτους λέγετε, θεοὺς ἢ ἄλλο τι γένος; ἄλλο τι ὡς εἰκὸς, τοὺς δαίμονας. πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ παλιλλογοῦντι τῷ Κέλσῳ (ἀνωτέρω γὰρ ἤδη πολλάκις ταῦτ᾿ αὐτῷ λέλεκται) οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἐπὶ πλεῖον διαλεχθῆναι· ἀρκέσει γὰρ τὰ εἰς τοῦθ᾿ ἡμῖν λελεγμένα. ὀλίγα δ᾿ ἀπὸ πλειόνων, ἃ δοκοῦμεν εἶναι συνᾴδοντα μὲν τοῖς προειρημένοις οὐ τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ πάντῃ ἐκείνοις ἔχοντα νοῦν, ἐκθησόμεθα· ἐν οἷς παραστήσομεν ὅτι καθολικῶς ἀποφηνάμενος θεὸν οὐδένα πρὸς ἀνθρώπους κατεληλυθέναι ἢ θεοῦ παῖδα ἀναιρεῖ καὶ τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν περὶ θεοῦ ἐπιφανείας δοξαζόμενα καὶ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω προειρημένα. εἰ γὰρ καθόλου λελεγμένον τὸ θεὸς καὶ θεοῦ παῖς οὐδεὶς κατῆλθεν οὐδὲ κατέλθοι ἀληθῶς τῷ Κέλσῳ εἴρηται, δηλονότι ἀνῄρηται τὸ εἶναι θεοὺς ἐπὶ γῆς, κατελθόντας ἐξ οὐρανοῦ. ἵνα ἤτοι μαντεύσωνται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἢ διὰ χρησμῶν θεραπεύσωσι, καὶ οὔτε ὁ Πύθιος οὔτ᾿ Ἀσκληπιὸς οὔτ᾿ ἄλλος τις τῶν νενομισμένων τὰ τοιαῦτα ποιεῖν θεὸς ἂν εἴη καταβὰς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, ἢ θεὸς μὲν εἴη ἂν ἀεὶ δὲ λαχὼν οἰκεῖν τὴν γῆν καὶ ὡσπερεὶ φυγὰς τοῦ τόπου τῶν θεῶν, ἤ τις τῶν μὴ ἐξουσίαν ἐχόντων κοινωνεῖν τοῖς ἐκεῖ θείοις εἴη ἂν. ἢ οὐ θεοὶ εἶεν ὁ Ἀπόλλων καὶ ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς καὶ ὅσοι ἐπὶ γῆς τι ποιεῖν πεπιστευμένοι εἰσὶν ἀλλά τινες δαίμονες, τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις σοφῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἁψῖδα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ διὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν ἀναβαινόντων πολλῷ χείρους.
thought_title: Celsus says no God comes down
pass_a_gloss: It lies before us (πρόκειται) now to overturn (ἀνατρέπω) his saying (λέξις) which is thus: 'God (θεός), O Jews and Christians, and child of God (θεοῦ παῖς), none (οὐδείς) either came down (κατέρχομαι, aor.) or would come down (opt.). And if you say some angels (ἄγγελοι), whom do you call these, gods or some other race/kind (γένος)? Some other, as is likely (ὡς εἰκός), the daemons (δαίμονες).' To Celsus repeating himself (παλιλλογέω) on these things (for above these things have already been said by him many times) it is not necessary to converse (διαλέγομαι) further; for what has been said by us on this will suffice. A few out of more, which we think agree (συνᾴδω) with what was said before but do not have wholly (πάντῃ) the same sense (νοῦς) as those, we shall set out; in which we shall show (παρίστημι) that, having declared (ἀποφαίνομαι) universally (καθολικῶς) that no god or child of god has come down to men, he abolishes (ἀναιρέω) both the things held (δοξάζω) by the many about the manifestation (ἐπιφάνεια) of god and the things said before by himself above. For if the universal statement 'god and child of god none came down nor would come down' has truly been said by Celsus, clearly it has been abolished that there are gods on earth having come down from heaven in order either to give oracles (μαντεύομαι) to men or to heal (θεραπεύω) through oracles (χρησμοί), and neither the Pythian (ὁ Πύθιος) nor Asclepius nor any other of those believed (νομίζω) to do such things would be a god having descended (καταβαίνω) from heaven; or he would be a god, but having been allotted (λαγχάνω) always to dwell on the earth and as it were an exile (φυγάς) from the place of the gods; or he would be one of those not having authority (ἐξουσία) to share (κοινωνέω) with the divine ones (θεῖοι) there. Or Apollo and Asclepius and as many as are believed (πιστεύω) to do something on earth would not be gods but certain daemons, much worse (χείρων) than the wise (σοφοί) among men who also ascend (ἀναβαίνω) to the vault (ἁψίς) of heaven through virtue (ἀρετή).

pass_b_english: Our task now, then, is to overturn his statement, which runs as follows: “No god, O Jews and Christians, and no son of God has come down, or would come down. But if you speak of certain angels, what do you call them: gods, or some other kind of being? Some other kind, presumably: the demons.”

Celsus is repeating himself here (for he has said these things many times already above), so there is no need to discuss them at greater length; what we have said on the point will suffice. Out of many things we shall set out a few, which we think agree with what was said before, yet do not carry entirely the same sense. In them we shall show that, by declaring universally that no god or son of God has come down to men, he does away both with what the multitude believe about the appearing of a god and with what he himself said earlier.

For if the statement Celsus has made universally, “No god and no son of God has come down, or would come down,” is true, then plainly it is ruled out that there are gods on earth, come down from heaven either to give oracles to men or to heal them through oracles. Then neither the Pythian god nor Asclepius nor any other of those believed to do such things could be a god who came down from heaven. Or else he would be a god, but one who had always had the earth as his allotted dwelling, like an exile from the place of the gods; or he would be one of those who have no right to share in the company of the divine beings there. Or else Apollo and Asclepius, and all who are believed to do anything on earth, would not be gods but some kind of demons, far worse than those wise men among mankind who, by their virtue, ascend even to the vault of heaven.
notes: Celsus’s words (θεὸς μὲν … τοὺς δαίμονας) are quoted again and answered in 5.4–5. ‘No son of God’ renders θεοῦ παῖς οὐδείς; lowercase ‘son’ because this is Celsus’s generic denial, while θεοῦ is kept as ‘God’ since he is denying the Christian claim. δαίμονες rendered ‘demons’ for consistency with the rest of this translation; in Celsus’s mouth the word is neutral, and Origen contests that in 5.5. ‘The Pythian god’ = Apollo of Delphi (ὁ Πύθιος; ‘god’ supplied from the article’s sense). ‘The vault of heaven’ (ἡ ἁψὶς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) echoes Plato, Phaedrus 247b (ἡ ὑπουράνιος ἁψίς); an echo, not a quotation, so not cited inline. ‘Appearing of a god’ renders θεοῦ ἐπιφάνεια (pagan epiphany). No Scripture in this chapter.
